entry: Landlocked U.S. state in the Mountain West (est. pop., 2024: 5,957,493). It is the eighth-largest state by area and encompasses most of the [[Rocky Mountains|Southern Rocky Mountains]]. President James Buchanan signed the act creating the Territory of Colorado on February 28, 1861, and the state was admitted to the Union as the 38th state on August 1, 1876. [[Denver]] is the capital and most populous city. Recreational [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] legalization in 2012 generated substantial tax revenue and sparked debate over social costs.

Major river of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. The 1,450-mile-long (2,330 km) river, the fifth-longest in the United States, drains an arid watershed of seven U.S. states and two Mexican states. Its name derives from the Spanish for *colored reddish*, reflecting its heavy silt load. Rising in the [[Rocky Mountains]], it flows through the [[Grand Canyon]], where a mid-19th-century expedition led by John Wesley Powell was the first to run the rapids. Dams, reservoirs and aqueducts divert almost its entire flow for [[Irrigation|irrigation]] and urban water supply, and its steep gradient generates [[Hydroelectricity|hydroelectricity]]. The largest of the major dams, [[Hoover Dam]], was completed in 1935. Intensive water consumption has dried up the lower 100 miles (160 km) of the river, which has rarely reached the sea since the 1960s. Since 2000, extended drought has conflicted with rising demand for its water.

City in east-central Colorado (pop., 2020: 478,961), county seat of El Paso County. It lies on Fountain Creek, 70 miles (113 km) south of [[Denver]], near the base of Pikes Peak, which rises 14,115 feet (4,302.31 m) on the eastern edge of the [[Rocky Mountains|Southern Rocky Mountains]]. The town was laid out in 1871 and incorporated on June 19, 1886. It is the state's second-most populous city and a key center for U.S. military and aerospace activities, including the U.S. Air Force Academy and Fort Carson.

Cancer of the colon or rectum, also called bowel cancer. Signs and symptoms may include blood in the stool, a change in bowel habits, weight loss, abdominal pain and fatigue. Risk factors include diet, [[Obesity|obesity]], [[Smoking|smoking]] and physical inactivity; red meat, processed meat and alcohol increase risk in the diet. Inherited disorders such as familial adenomatous polyposis account for less than 5% of cases. The cancer typically begins as a benign polyp that becomes cancerous over time. Screening of average-risk adults aged 45–75 effectively prevents the disease and reduces deaths. Treatment may combine [[Surgery|surgery]], [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]], [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] and targeted therapy; cancer confined to the colon wall may be curable with surgery, but widespread cancer usually is not. The five-year survival rate in the United States is approximately 65.4% (data from 2016–2022). In 2022, there were 1.93 million new cases and 903,859 deaths worldwide, making it the third-most common cancer.

Species of very large [[Squid|squid]], believed to be the largest by mass. Its confirmed mass is at least 495 kilograms (1,091 lb), and its maximum total length is approximately 4.2 metres (14 ft). *Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni*, the only recognized member of its genus, belongs to the family Cranchiidae. It has the largest eyes of any documented animal, about 27–30 cm (11–12 in) across, and is the only member of its family with hooks on its arms. It inhabits the circumantarctic [[Southern Ocean]], where it is presumed to be an ambush predator and is likely a key prey item of the [[Sperm whale|sperm whale]].

Ancient Roman amphitheater in central Rome, Italy. Known as the Flavian Amphitheatre, it was begun under Emperor Vespasian in AD 72 and completed under his successor Titus in AD 80, with later modifications under [[Domitian]]. Built of travertine, [[Tuff|tuff]] and Roman concrete, it could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators. It hosted [[Gladiator|gladiatorial]] contests, animal hunts and executions, as well as re-enactments of famous battles and dramas based on [[Roman mythology]]. Earthquakes and stone robbers ruined much of it, and it was later reused as housing, workshops, a fortress and a quarry. It remains one of the best-known symbols of Imperial Rome and one of Rome's most popular tourist attractions. Each Good Friday, the [[Pope|pope]] leads a torchlit Catholic procession in the area around it.

[[Bronze]] statue of the Greek sun god Helios, on the Greek island of [[Rhodes]]. One of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]], it was built by Chares of Lindos in 280 BC to celebrate the defense of Rhodes against Demetrius I of Macedon. It stood approximately 70 [[Cubit|cubits]], or 33 metres (108 feet), making it the tallest statue in the ancient world. An earthquake toppled it in 226 BC, and the Rhodians did not rebuild it, in accordance with the Oracle of Delphi. Its height was approximately two-thirds that of the [[Statue of Liberty]] from feet to crown.

American film production and distribution company, the flagship unit of the [[Sony Pictures]] Motion Picture Group. Founded in 1918 as Cohn-Brandt-Cohn Film Sales Corporation by Jack and Harry Cohn and Joe Brandt, it adopted the Columbia Pictures name in 1924. A successful association with director [[Frank Capra]] spurred growth from the late 1920s, and *It Happened One Night* (1934) won the studio its first Academy Award for Best Picture. Its library of more than 3,500 titles includes 12 Best Picture winners, more than any other studio. The [[Coca-Cola]] Company acquired the studio in 1982, and [[Sony]] acquired it in 1989.

American record label owned by [[Sony]] Music Entertainment. Founded in 1889 as the Columbia Phonograph Company in Washington, D.C., it is the oldest surviving brand name in the recorded sound business. It pioneered the long-playing (LP) record in 1948. The [[CBS]] network owned the label from 1938 to 1988, when Sony acquired CBS Records for approximately $2 billion. Its artists have included [[Louis Armstrong]], [[Miles Davis]], [[Bob Dylan]] and [[Bruce Springsteen]].

Largest river in the [[Pacific Northwest]] region of North America. It rises in the [[Rocky Mountains]] of [[British Columbia]], Canada, and flows 1,243 miles (2,000 km) northwest, then south into Washington and west along most of the Washington–Oregon border to the [[Pacific Ocean]]. Its [[Drainage basin|drainage basin]] is about the size of France, extending into seven U.S. states and one Canadian province. On May 11, 1792, the American ship *Columbia Rediviva*, under Captain Robert Gray, became the first non-indigenous vessel to enter the river. The 14 hydroelectric [[Dam|dams]] on its main stem and many tributaries produce more than 44 percent of total U.S. hydroelectric generation. Plutonium for [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] was produced at the Hanford Site, now the most contaminated nuclear site in the United States. Dams and industrial pollution have blocked fish migration and altered the river environment.

City, capital of [[South Carolina]] (pop., 2020: 136,632) and county seat of [[County (United States)|Richland County]]. It is the state's second-most populous city. Established in 1786 as South Carolina's first planned capital, it lies at the fall line where the Broad and Saluda rivers form the Congaree River. During the [[American Civil War]], much of the city was destroyed in the burning of Columbia in 1865, and it was rebuilt during Reconstruction. It is home to the University of South Carolina and Fort Jackson, the U.S. Army's largest basic combat training installation.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in [[New York City]]. Established in 1754 as King's College by royal charter from [[George II of Great Britain|George II]], it is the oldest institution of higher education in New York and the fifth-oldest in the United States. Renamed Columbia College in 1784 after the American Revolution, it moved to its current campus and became Columbia University in 1896. Its trustees in 1787 were headed by former students [[Alexander Hamilton]] and John Jay. The university administers and annually awards the [[Pulitzer Prize]]. As of December 2021, its alumni, faculty and staff included 103 Nobel laureates. Its researchers contributed to early planning for the [[Manhattan Project]] during [[World War II]]. Since October 2023, its handling of pro-Palestinian protests and reported incidents of antisemitism has prompted federal civil rights investigations, and its president resigned in August 2024.

Widespread transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Old and New Worlds, beginning in the late 15th century. Named after the Italian explorer [[Christopher Columbus]], it was tied to European colonization and global trade after his 1492 voyage. Diseases of Old World origin reduced the Indigenous population of the [[Americas]] by 80 to 95 percent. Crops such as [[Maize|maize]], [[Potato|potatoes]], [[Tobacco|tobacco]] and chili peppers became important worldwide, while Old World [[Rice|rice]], wheat, [[Sugarcane|sugar cane]] and livestock became important in the Americas. The number of Africans taken to the New World far exceeded the number of Europeans who moved there in the first three centuries after Columbus. Historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term in 1972 in his book *The Columbian Exchange*.

Bird family of doves and pigeons, the only family in the order Columbiformes. Members are stout-bodied, with small heads, short necks and slender bills. The family contains 52 genera and 353 species, and most species eat seeds and fruit. Doves are usually the smaller species and pigeons the larger, although the distinction is not scientific. The domestic pigeon descends from the wild [[Rock dove]]. Most species are monogamous, and parents feed their chicks crop milk, a nutrient-rich secretion from the esophagus. Of the family's species, 118 (34%) are at risk and 13 are extinct, including the [[Dodo]] and the [[Passenger pigeon]], which once flocked in the billions.

1999 school shooting and attempted bombing in Columbine, Colorado, U.S. On April 20, 1999, two senior students, [[Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold]], killed students and a teacher at Columbine High School and injured 20 others before dying by [[Suicide|suicide]]. It was the deadliest K–12 school shooting in U.S. history until the [[Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting]] in December 2012. The attack led to the immediate action rapid deployment (IARD) tactic for active-shooter situations. As of June 2025, it had inspired more than 70 copycat crimes, a phenomenon called the Columbine effect.

American crime drama television series. [[Peter Falk]] stars as Lieutenant Columbo, a Los Angeles [[Homicide|homicide]] detective who often returns with the catchphrase "Just one more thing" to ask a critical question. Created by Richard Levinson and William Link, the series popularized the inverted detective format, in which the audience sees the crime and its perpetrator at the outset. It aired on [[NBC]] from 1971 to 1978 and on ABC from 1989 to 2003. Falk won four Primetime Emmy Awards for the role. Villains have included [[Donald Pleasence]] and [[Dick Van Dyke]].

Capital of the U.S. state of [[Ohio]] (pop., 2020: 905,748). It is the 14th-most populous U.S. city and the second-most populous in the Midwest, after Chicago. Founded in 1812 at the confluence of the Scioto and Olentangy rivers, it was named after [[Christopher Columbus]] and became the state capital in 1816. By the 2020s the city had become a major center for high technology and advanced manufacturing, particularly [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]], [[Robotics|robotics]] and semiconductor fabrication. It is home to Ohio State University.

Vertical structural element in [[Architecture|architecture]] and engineering, carrying weight from above to below by compression. Columns usually have a base, a shaft and a capital, and they support beams, arches or upper walls and roofs. A small wooden or metal support is typically called a post, while a non-round support is usually called a pier. Early examples appeared in Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3000 BC. In [[Ancient Greece]], the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders developed during the Archaic period (c. 800–480 BC), and the Romans added the Tuscan and Composite orders. A long sequence of columns joined by an entablature is called a colonnade.

Prolonged state of deep unconsciousness with no response to pain, light or sound. A patient in a coma lacks a sleep–wake cycle, cannot initiate voluntary actions and does not respond normally to stimuli. Clinically, a coma is the consistent inability to follow a one-step command. Consciousness depends on the [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]] and the reticular activating system in the [[Brainstem|brainstem]]. Causes include trauma, [[Stroke|stroke]], metabolic disorders such as [[Hypoglycemia|hypoglycemia]], infections and drug overdoses; comas can also be medically induced, as during general anesthesia. The Glasgow Coma Scale scores consciousness from 3 (deepest coma) to 15 (fully alert). Complications include [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] and blood clots, and prolonged coma beyond weeks raises the risk of death, [[Vegetative state|persistent vegetative state]] or long-term disability.

Selection of distinct items from a set, in which order does not matter. Unlike a [[Permutation|permutation]], a combination is a subset of k distinct elements. For example, an apple, an orange and a pear give three combinations of two fruits: an apple and a pear, an apple and an orange, or a pear and an orange. The number of k-combinations of an n-element set is the [[Binomial coefficient|binomial coefficient]], written C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!). Combinations underpin the [[Binomial theorem|binomial theorem]]. In probability, they count outcomes, such as the 3,744 possible full house hands in five-card poker from a standard deck.

Branch of discrete mathematics concerned with counting and with the properties of finite structures. It is closely related to many areas, from logic to statistical physics and from evolutionary biology to [[Computer science|computer science]]. Its problems arise in [[Algebra|algebra]], [[Probability theory|probability theory]], topology and geometry. One of its oldest parts is [[Graph theory|graph theory]]. Modern work began in the 17th century with [[Blaise Pascal]] and [[Jacob Bernoulli]], who applied counting to probability. In the later 20th century, general theoretical methods made combinatorics an independent branch of mathematics. Its subfields include enumerative, algebraic and extremal combinatorics.

Agricultural machine that harvests grain crops such as [[Wheat|wheat]], [[Rice|rice]] and [[Maize|maize]]. Its name reflects how it combined reaping, threshing and winnowing into one process around the start of the 20th century. It is among the most economically important labor-saving inventions, greatly reducing the share of the population employed in agriculture. The first practical combine was patented in 1836 by Hiram Moore and John Hascall in the United States; it was horse-drawn. The first self-propelled combine was introduced by Holt in 1911. Modern machines have four main parts: an intake mechanism, a threshing and separation system, a cleaning system, and grain handling and storage. Combines accounted for the majority of grain harvests in North America, Europe and Australia.

Oral form of combined hormonal [[Birth control|contraception]], containing [[Estrogen|estrogen]] and a progestin. When taken correctly, it alters the [[Menstrual cycle|menstrual cycle]] to stop ovulation and prevent [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. It was first approved for contraceptive use in the United States in 1960, and more than 100 million women worldwide use it, including about 9 million in the United States. Effectiveness is 99% with perfect use and about 91% with typical use. Non-contraceptive uses include regulating menstrual cycles and treating [[Acne|acne]]. Risks include a three- to sixfold increase in venous thromboembolism, particularly in the first year of use and among smokers and women over 35. The pill is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines and was a catalyst for the [[Sexual revolution|sexual revolution]].

High-temperature exothermic [[Redox|redox]] reaction between a fuel and an oxidant, usually atmospheric oxygen. It often produces light as a flame or glow, and a flame indicates that the reaction is occurring. Activation energy must be supplied to start combustion, but the heat of a flame can keep the reaction self-sustaining. The combination of hydrogen and oxygen into water vapor (H₂O), which releases 242 kJ/mol of heat, fuels [[Rocket engine|rocket engines]]. Complete combustion of hydrocarbons yields mainly [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and water, while incomplete combustion produces [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] and [[Soot|soot]]. Burning in air also creates nitrogen oxides, so [[Catalytic converter|catalytic converters]] may be required by law. Combustion remains the main method of producing energy for humanity, from fossil fuels such as coal and oil or from renewable fuels such as firewood.

American multinational [[Telecommunications|telecommunications]] and media conglomerate, headquartered in [[Philadelphia]]. It is the largest home Internet service provider in the United States and the second-largest [[Cable television|cable]] TV company by subscribers. Through NBCUniversal, its media holdings include [[NBC]] and [[Universal Pictures]], and it has been the parent company of Sky Group since 2018. In June 2026 Comcast announced plans to spin off NBCUniversal and Sky, with completion expected in summer 2027. Critics note limited competition, and its ownership of both content and distribution has raised antitrust concerns that scuttled a 2014 effort to acquire Time Warner Cable.
